UNIT 21: POPULATION CHANGE
Key theme: population change looks at the rise and fall of population over time.
Learning outcome 2.8: describe and explain how birth rates, ageing, gender equality, rural depopulation and migration affect population change, and apply these to Ireland, India and a local setting (Gorey, Co. Wexford).

KEY WORDS
- Natural increase: more births than deaths, so the population grows naturally.
- Natural decrease: more deaths than births, so the population declines naturally.
- Birth rate: the number of births (usually per 1,000 people per year).
- Death rate: the number of deaths (usually per 1,000 people per year).
- Net migration: the total number of immigrants minus the total number of emigrants.
- Immigration: people moving into a country.
- Emigration: people leaving a country.
- Internal migration: the movement of people within a country.
- Ageing: the increase in the number of older people in the population, usually because people live longer and birth rates fall, so the average age rises.
- Gender equality: men and women having similar access to education, jobs and political representation.
- Rural depopulation: a drop in the number of people living in rural areas.
- Replacement level: a total fertility rate of 2.1 children per woman, needed to keep a population steady (without migration).
- Total fertility rate (TFR): average number of children per woman.
- Marriage bar: law that required women in the civil service and some other jobs to resign once they married. Lifted in Ireland in 1973.
- Gender pay gap: the difference in average earnings between men and women, as a percentage of men's earnings (e.g. men earn 1.00 euro, women 0.87 euro = gap of 13%).
- STEM: Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics.
- Infant mortality: the death of an infant within the first year of its life.
- Literacy rate: the number of people who can read and write.
- Donor region: the area people leave when they migrate; it 'donates' people.
- Receiver region: the area that receives migrants and gains people.
- Diaspora: the spread of people from their original homeland.
- Dependency ratio: the balance between dependants (young and old) and people of working age.
- Silver economy: businesses that focus on caring for the elderly.
- Brain drain: emigration of young, skilled people. Brain gain: inward migration of skilled people.

TWO MAIN REASONS A POPULATION CHANGES
- 1. Natural change: the difference between births and deaths.
- 2. Net migration: the difference between immigration and emigration.
- Formula: Population Change = Birth Rates - Death Rates + Net Migration.
- Worked example (simple numbers): 60,000 births - 35,000 deaths + 20,000 net migration = population grows by 45,000.

POPULATION CHANGE IN IRELAND - OVERVIEW
- About 2.9 million in 1950; about 5.4 million in 2025; projected about 5.6 million by 2030.
- Geofact: the global total fertility rate has halved in the last 60 years.

IRELAND: BIRTH RATES
- Early 1980s: about 2.6 children per woman. Today: closer to 1.5 - below the replacement level of 2.1.
- Falling birth rates mean fewer young people and more older adults.
- Economic and social factors: people delay children to focus on education and career; couples want financial stability first; soaring housing and childcare costs make more than one or two children hard to afford; welfare payments (paid maternity/paternity and parental leave, child benefit) affect decisions on family size.
- Changes in Irish culture: in the past the Catholic Church strongly influenced contraceptive use, leading to bigger families; today many choose smaller families; changing gender roles mean many women focus on careers first.
- Average age of first-time mothers: 26 in the 1980s, over 31 today. Lower TFR plus later motherhood = fewer babies each year.
- Government family supports: free GP care for under-eights, the National Childcare Scheme (NCS), increased maternity and parental leave. (Figure 21.1: HSE campaign for free GP visit cards for 6- and 7-year-olds.)

IRELAND: AGEING
- 2022: about 15.7% aged 65 or older; predicted to almost double to 30% by 2050. One of the most significant population changes in Ireland's history.
- Impacts on population: higher life expectancy plus low birth rates = fewer children, more older people; growth slows; more dependent on migration. CSO projects deaths will outnumber births by 2040, so growth will rely almost entirely on immigration.
- Impacts on economy: life expectancy about 83 years (better healthcare, living standards, diet). Number aged 85+ expected to rise by over 270% by 2051.
- Fewer workers producing goods, paying taxes and supporting services. 2026: 4 working-age adults per person over 65 (4:1); by 2050 could be 2:1.
- Age-related costs expected to rise by about 6% of national income by 2050 - over 16 billion euro. The Future Ireland Fund is a savings fund to help pay future age-related costs, but experts say savings alone are not enough; pension changes needed.
- Geofacts: CSO says over-65s will exceed 1 million by 2030 and 1.81 million by 2057. State Pension age is 66; since 2024 people can defer pension up to age 70 for a higher weekly rate.
- Meeting the challenge: raising the retirement age keeps more people working, supports the economy, keeps pensions sustainable and reduces the burden on the next generation.
- Healthy Age Friendly Homes programme (Age Friendly Ireland and the HSE): helps people 65+ live safely and independently in their own homes, reducing strain on hospitals and nursing homes.
- Figure 21.4 (Social Justice Ireland, Future Demography of Ireland): population 5.4 million (2025) to 6.6 million (2051), an extra 1.2 million. Share aged 65+: 13.3% (2016), 18.1% (2031), 24.6% (2051). Working-age people per person 65+: 5 (2016), 3.4 (2025), 2.5 (2051).

IRELAND: GENDER EQUALITY
- 2025: Ireland ranked 10th of 148 countries on the Global Gender Gap Index, score 80.1%.
- Women are about 47% of the workforce and over half of third-level students. One in four company board members and nearly one in three TDs are women.
- Gender pay gap fell from 14% (2012) to below 9% (2024).
- Women attaining third-level education rose from below 38% (2011) to over 50% (2023).
- The marriage bar (until the 1970s): women in certain jobs had to resign on marriage. This kept women out of paid work, focused on large families, so birth rates were very high; smaller family incomes and slower economic growth.
- 1973: marriage bar removed. 1975: equal pay for equal work laws. More women in third-level and working outside the home; to balance work, education and family, women had fewer children and family size fell.
- 2017: National Strategy for Women and Girls - fairer workplaces, close the pay gap, support women in STEM. Women still hold fewer senior roles.
- Government support: paid parental leave, NCS, flexible working - easier to combine work and family; reduces dependency ratio and keeps more people employed for longer. Female life expectancy 84.5 years, one of the highest in Europe.
- Reproductive healthcare and free contraception help couples plan families, so population growth is more stable and predictable.
- Result: stable population growth, economic development and reduced effects of ageing.

IRELAND: RURAL DEPOPULATION
- Young people leave for towns and cities for jobs and better quality of life, leaving smaller, older communities. It alters population structure.
- The Great Famine caused rural population to fall drastically through out-migration; people went abroad or to Dublin, Cork, Belfast; rural population kept falling for more than a century.
- 1883-1936: government scheme built small labourers' cottages to house families and encourage rural population growth (helped in some areas). Depopulation continued in the remote west and midlands (few jobs, poor infrastructure). Figure 21.6: derelict labourer's cottage, Co. Sligo.
- By the 1980s: rural areas far from cities (Mayo, Donegal, Sligo) still declining; towns with better transport grew, e.g. Maynooth, Co. Kildare grew 16.6% (2011-2016) due to transport links, colleges and jobs.
- National population is highest since 1851, but growth is mainly in the east and southeast; west and midlands still losing people. Rural Ireland is about 35% of the population and many areas are greying faster, with more over-65s than the national average.
- Effects: loss of schools, shops, post offices and services in the west. Push factors: loss of services, lack of jobs (especially STEM), poor transport, unreliable internet. Cities attract in-migration (work, colleges, social services).
- Government support: Project Ireland 2040 and Our Rural Future. Rural Regeneration and Development Fund (RRDF): creates jobs and promotes remote working by improving housing, broadband and public spaces in towns under 10,000 people.
- Rural decline has slowed since 2016 near cities (e.g. Galway city), but marginal western areas like Connemara still lose people and services. Stronger planning and targeted investment needed.

IRELAND: MIGRATION
- Migration reshapes population structure, increases cultural diversity, strengthens the workforce and influences where people live.
- 19th and early 20th centuries: millions emigrated to the US, Britain and beyond (poverty, unemployment).
- Today a wealthy economy attracts workers, students and settlers. EU freedom of movement and global events (e.g. the war in Ukraine) influence who comes.
- Migration was the main cause of population change 2016-2024. Year to April 2024: largest annual increase in 16 years - nearly 99,000. Immigrants are mostly aged 25-44, adding to the working population and reducing the effects of ageing. (Summary: over 149,000 arrivals in 2024.)
- Internal migration: 1996-2022 many moved from Dublin to Wicklow, Kildare and Meath (cheaper housing, better road and rail). Rural-to-urban migration causes decline in the remote west and north-west, leaving an ageing population.
- Department of Finance projection: population could be 5.8 to 6.8 million by 2050.

IRELAND: POPULATION CHANGE SINCE THE 1960s (Figure 21.9 timeline)
- 1960s: population began to grow for the first time in over 120 years. Government policies attracted MNCs and FDI, created jobs, reduced emigration, encouraged inward migration.
- 1973: joined the EU (then EEC) - larger markets, more trade, higher incomes; attracted migrants and encouraged people to stay.
- 1980s: recession and high unemployment; over 200,000 mainly young adults emigrated (brain drain); growth slowed.
- 1995-2008 Celtic Tiger: rapid economic growth, rising living standards, jobs, significant inward migration (brain gain). Population 3.9 million by 2002, from both migration and natural increase.
- Post-2008: global financial crisis caused severe downturn; renewed emigration of young adults; birth rate stayed fairly high so growth continued more slowly.
- 2016: population 4.7 million; highest birth rate in the EU (13.9 per 1,000) and lowest death rate (6.9 per 1,000) - a modern 'baby boom'.
- 2025: about 5.46 million, driven by net inward migration plus natural increase; immigration is now the most important factor as fertility falls.
- 2050 projection (CSO): 5.8 to 6.8 million depending on migration.

INDIA: OVERVIEW
- Population 1.46 billion - over four times bigger than in 1950; projected 1.52 billion by 2030.
- Figure 21.10 (2001-2011 change by state): e.g. Bihar +25.4%, Kerala lower growth (about +4.9%), Nagaland -0.6%, Uttar Pradesh +20.2%, Delhi +21.2%. Northern states grew faster than southern ones.

INDIA: BIRTH RATES
- 1960s: women had about six children, especially in rural northern states (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar). Children were an economic asset (farm work, chores). Poor healthcare and sanitation caused high infant mortality, so parents had more children to ensure some survived.
- Kerala (south): government spending on education and healthcare raised literacy and living standards; parents grew confident children would survive; by the 1980s women had 2-3 children. Shows education and living standards reduce birth rates.
- TFR: about 6.1 (1950s), 3.4 (1990s), about 2.1 (2025). (The ageing section and summary give about 1.9 now.) Falling birth rates slowed growth and reduced pressure on schools, housing and healthcare.
- Economic and social progress: rural-to-urban migration raises costs of housing, childcare and education; parents choose fewer children to invest more in each.
- India was one of the first countries with a government-led family planning programme (1950s): posters, radio ads, symbols on buildings (Figure 21.14: elephant and mural with family planning symbol, 1970s); contraception and voluntary sterilisation.
- Regional differences: south (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra) lower birth rates; north (Bihar, Uttar Pradesh) higher - reflecting education, income, healthcare and culture.
- Figure 21.13: 42.7% of Indians under 25; 50.2% aged 25-64; 7.1% aged 65+.

INDIA: AGEING
- About 7% aged 65+. UN and World Bank: by 2050 one in five Indians (20-25%) will be over 60. India moving from a young country to an ageing society.
- Fertility about 1.9 (below replacement). Life expectancy about 70 thanks to better nutrition, sanitation and healthcare.
- Growth continues but slower; natural increase will slow; population may level out or decline after 2050; higher old-age dependency ratio.
- Figure 21.16: share aged 60+ was 10.7% (2023), projected 20.8% (2050) and 36.1% (2100).
- Challenges: only 29% of Indians receive a pension, so many elderly depend on family or public schemes.
- Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act: legally obliges children and heirs to care for older relatives. UN Population Fund campaigns for investment in healthcare, housing and social protection for the elderly in Global South countries.
- Silver economy: geriatric healthcare, retirement homes, assistive technology - big growth sectors.

INDIA: GENDER EQUALITY
- 2025: ranked 131st of 148 on the Global Gender Gap Index, score 64.1%.
- Women about 29% of workforce, just over half of third-level graduates; about 8% of CEOs and 13% of MPs are women; women earn about 70% of what men earn for similar work.
- Until the 1960s most women married young and had five or six children; girls left school early; women rarely worked outside the home; very fast growth.
- 1980s-1990s: government promoted family planning and girls' education; birth rates fell; cities (Delhi, Chennai, Mumbai) offered jobs for women. Kerala and Tamil Nadu slowed first.
- 2015: Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao ('Save the Daughter, Educate the Daughter') promoted female equality and challenged 'son preference'. Urban Delhi now averages 1.2 children per woman.
- Today almost all girls attend school; but workplace barriers remain (text gives 46% of women in the workforce; 20% of board members and 13% of government representatives are women).
- Laws: Equal Remuneration Act and Maternity Benefit Act - but poorly enforced in rural and informal workplaces. Needed: longer maternity leave, better childcare, equal pay.
- Empowering women leads to fewer children, more investment per child, lower birth and infant mortality rates, higher life expectancy, slower growth, better economy - most evident in urban areas.
- Uttar Pradesh and Bihar: some of the highest birth rates, linked to some of the lowest female education and workforce rates; gender-based violence, discrimination and lack of support for working mothers slow progress.
- Steps for improvement: more education for girls (rural), equal pay and childcare, family-friendly workplaces, more women in leadership and politics.
- Figure 21.21: India's birth rate per 1,000 has stayed well above Ireland's from 1960-2020, though both have fallen.

INDIA: RURAL DEPOPULATION
- Rural share: over 82% (1960) to about 63.6% (2023).
- Main cause: out-migration of young people for education and jobs, e.g. from Uttar Pradesh and Bihar; leaves fewer young and more older people; lower rural population density, especially in harsh, less productive areas.
- 1951-2011: rural population still grew, but rate slowed from over 20% per decade (1950s-1970s) to 12.3% (2001-2011). Wealthy coastal or agriculturally rich rural areas stable or growing; interior regions declined.
- Cities like Mumbai and Delhi face overcrowding. India becoming more urban.

INDIA: MIGRATION
- 2001-2011: about 5.65 million people migrated within India every year, mostly for work.
- Donor regions: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar. Receiver region: Maharashtra (Mumbai) - services, construction, industry. Major destination cities: Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata.
- About one in three city dwellers is a migrant; most move for work or marriage. Men: jobs. Women: culture, especially arranged marriages (brides move to husbands' families).
- Effects: birth rates fall in rural donor areas and rise in cities; overcrowding and pressure on housing, transport and services; slums sprawl in Mumbai.
- Emigration: world's largest diaspora - nearly 18 million abroad (UAE, US, Saudi Arabia, UK). About 2.5 million emigrate each year, often for skilled jobs in technology, engineering, healthcare.
- War and disasters: in 2024, 60,000 people left Manipur due to ethnic conflict.
- Age: most migrants aged 18-40 - boosts city working-age population; leaves rural areas with children and older adults (high dependency ratio).
- Gender: rural-urban migration mostly male; marriage migration mostly female; affects rural gender balance.
- Size: slows rural growth, helps cities and the economy grow.

CASE STUDY: GOREY, CO. WEXFORD (LOCAL SETTING)
- One of the fastest-growing towns in Wexford: up 26.4% to 11,517 (2011-2022), twice the growth of any other Wexford town.
- Popular with remote workers and commuters to Dublin, Wicklow and Wexford; affordable housing and new motorway attracted young families; rapid housing, younger population, more need for schools. Gorey Community School is the largest secondary school in Ireland.
- Fewer children per family; average age of first-time mothers over 33.
- More older adults; retirees move to coastal areas like Ballymoney, Courtown, Kilmuckridge.
- More women than men (jobs in services and education).
- Migration is the main driver of growth; international migrants from Poland and Lithuania.
- Table 2011 vs 2022: population 9,114 to 11,517; birth rate about 15.7 to about 11.3 per 1,000; aged 65+ 9.5% to 12.3%; male:female 4,427:4,687 (94.4 males per 100 females) to 5,567:5,950 (93.6 per 100). 2022 age groups: 0-17 27.2%, 18-64 60.5%, 65+ 12.3%; males 48.3%, females 51.7%.
- Future planning: affordable housing and transport for commuters; schools and childcare; GP, health and social services for older people. Gorey to become a more important regional service hub. Reflects national and global trends.

EXAM SKILLS: IRELAND 1975-2025 (SEC sample paper style answer)
- Post-1973 EU membership and FDI policy boosted jobs and reduced emigration.
- Late 1970s-1990s: negative net migration 1978-1996; over 200,000 young adults emigrated to Britain, US, Canada, Australia (brain drain), despite high birth rates. 1989: population change negative. Emigrants of child-bearing age helped drop fertility to about 2.3.
- Celtic Tiger 1995-2008: FDI from Apple, Google, Boston Scientific; brain gain; returning Irish; EU workers. Growth peaked in 2005 with a net increase of 90,000. Natural increase rose because more people in their 20s and 30s lived here, not because women had more children; housing boom.
- 2008 crash: banking and housing crisis; by 2010 almost 30,000 more left than arrived.
- 2016: 4.7 million, baby boom (13.9 births, 6.9 deaths per 1,000).
- Since 2020: recovery; migrants from Europe and India; refugees from Ukraine and Syria; 2025 population about 5.46 million, up about 80,000 in one year; migration now the main driver.

rows.prompt: What is natural change in a population?
options: The rise in the average age of a population
The difference between births and deaths
The difference between immigration and emigration
The movement of people within a country
rows.explanation: Natural change is births minus deaths; net migration covers people moving in and out.

rows.prompt: A country has 50,000 births, 30,000 deaths and net migration of +10,000. What is the population change?
rows.explanation: Using Births - Deaths + Net Migration: 50,000 - 30,000 + 10,000 = 30,000.

rows.prompt: What does net migration mean?
rows.explanation: Net migration is the total number of immigrants minus the total number of emigrants.

rows.prompt: What is the replacement level fertility rate?
rows.explanation: A TFR of 2.1 is needed to keep a population steady without migration.

rows.prompt: About how many children does the average Irish woman have today?
rows.explanation: Ireland's TFR fell from about 2.6 in the early 1980s to close to 1.5 today.

rows.explanation: It rose from 26 in the 1980s to over 31 today.

rows.explanation: Free GP care for under-eights, the NCS and longer leave help parents balance work and family.

rows.explanation: About 15.7% were 65+ in 2022, predicted to almost double to 30% by 2050.

rows.explanation: The CSO projects that by 2040 deaths will begin to outnumber births, so growth will rely on immigration.

rows.prompt: Name the two main reasons why a population changes and write the formula for population change.
rows.model_answer: The two reasons are natural change (births minus deaths) and net migration (immigrants minus emigrants). Population Change = Birth Rates - Death Rates + Net Migration.

rows.prompt: Explain two reasons why Ireland's birth rate has fallen over the last 50 years.
rows.model_answer: People delay having children to focus on education and careers and to be financially stable first. High housing and childcare costs make it hard to afford more than one or two children. The Catholic Church's influence on contraception has weakened, so many choose smaller families.

rows.prompt: Describe two impacts of an ageing population on Ireland's economy.
rows.model_answer: As more people retire there are fewer workers producing goods, paying taxes and supporting public services; the ratio could fall from 4:1 in 2026 to 2:1 by 2050. Paying for pensions and healthcare will be costly - about 6% of national income or over 16 billion euro by 2050.

rows.prompt: Explain how gender equality has changed family size in Ireland.
rows.model_answer: Before 1973 the marriage bar kept many women at home raising large families. After it was lifted and equal pay laws came in (1975), more women went to third level and worked outside the home. To balance work, education and family, women had fewer children and family size fell.

rows.prompt: Name three push factors that cause people to leave rural Ireland.
rows.model_answer: Loss of services such as schools, shops and post offices; a lack of jobs, especially in STEM; poor transport; and unreliable internet connection.

rows.prompt: Explain why birth rates were high in rural northern India in the 1960s.
rows.model_answer: Children were an economic asset who helped with farm work and chores. Poor healthcare and sanitation caused high infant mortality, so parents had more children to make sure some survived to adulthood. Women married young and girls left school early.

rows.prompt: Describe how internal migration affects population structure in India's rural donor regions and its cities.
rows.model_answer: Most migrants are aged 18-40, so cities gain working-age people while rural areas are left with children and older adults, giving a high dependency ratio. Birth rates fall in rural donor areas and rise in cities. Because rural-urban migration is mostly male, some rural areas have a gender imbalance, while cities like Mumbai suffer overcrowding and slums.

rows.prompt: Using Gorey, Co. Wexford, describe two features of population change in a local setting.
rows.model_answer: Gorey grew by 26.4% to 11,517 between 2011 and 2022, mainly through migration of commuters, remote workers and migrants from Poland and Lithuania. Its share aged 65+ rose from 9.5% to 12.3% as retirees moved to coastal areas like Courtown, while the birth rate fell from about 15.7 to 11.3 per 1,000.

rows.prompt: Discuss the trends in Ireland's population change since 1975. Your answer should refer to both natural change and net migration. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: After joining the EU in 1973 Ireland gained larger markets, and policies attracting MNCs and FDI created jobs and reduced emigration. However, from the late 1970s to the 1990s recession and high unemployment caused negative net migration (1978-1996), with over 200,000 young adults emigrating to Britain, the US, Canada and Australia - a brain drain. Birth rates were still high, but in 1989 population change was negative, and the loss of people of child-bearing age helped lower fertility to about 2.3. During the Celtic Tiger (1995-2008) FDI from firms like Apple and Google created jobs, bringing returning Irish and EU workers (brain gain). Population reached 3.9 million by 2002 and growth peaked in 2005 at 90,000. Natural increase rose because more people in their 20s and 30s lived here. The 2008 crash brought renewed emigration; by 2010 almost 30,000 more left than arrived. Yet in 2016 Ireland had the EU's highest birth rate (13.9) and lowest death rate (6.9 per 1,000). Since 2020 migration from Europe, India, Ukraine and Syria has driven growth to about 5.46 million in 2025, as fertility falls and mothers are older.
rows.marking_scheme: Discussion of trends: 15 SRPs x 2m = 30m. Credit SRPs for: EU membership/FDI; negative net migration 1978-1996 with statistic; brain drain/destinations; high birth rate but negative change 1989; fertility to 2.3; Celtic Tiger and named MNCs; brain gain/return migration; 3.9 million by 2002; peak 2005; natural increase linked to age structure; 2008 crash and emigration; 2010 figure; 2016 birth/death rates; post-2020 migrants named; 2025 total; falling fertility. Must refer to both natural change and net migration for full marks.

rows.prompt: Examine the impact of an ageing population on Ireland and the measures taken to meet this challenge. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Ireland's population is ageing because life expectancy has risen to about 83 years and the fertility rate has fallen to about 1.5, below replacement level. In 2022 about 15.7% of people were 65+, predicted to almost double to 30% by 2050, and the number aged 85+ could rise by over 270% by 2051. Population growth will slow and the CSO projects that deaths will outnumber births by 2040, so growth will depend on immigration. The economy will be affected because fewer workers will pay taxes and support services: the ratio of working-age adults to over-65s could fall from 4:1 in 2026 to 2:1 by 2050. Age-related costs could rise by about 6% of national income, over 16 billion euro, by 2050. To meet this challenge the government set up the Future Ireland Fund to save for these costs. Raising the retirement age keeps people working longer; since 2024 people can defer their pension to 70. The Healthy Age Friendly Homes programme helps older people live independently at home, reducing pressure on hospitals and nursing homes. Family supports such as the NCS and parental leave keep more women working, reducing the dependency ratio, while immigrants aged 25-44 also strengthen the workforce.

rows.prompt: Describe and explain how gender equality has influenced population change in a Global South country you have studied. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: In India, until the 1960s most women married young, left school early and had five or six children, so growth was very fast. In the 1980s and 1990s the government promoted family planning and girls' education. Educated women learned about health and family planning and worked in cities like Delhi and Mumbai, so birth rates fell, first in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. The 2015 Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao scheme challenged son preference, and urban Delhi now averages 1.2 children per woman. However, India ranked only 131st of 148 on the Global Gender Gap Index in 2025, women are about 29% of the workforce and earn about 70% of men's pay. Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, with low female education, still have some of the highest birth rates.

rows.prompt: Explain how rural depopulation has affected population change in Ireland. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Rural depopulation is a drop in the number of people living in rural areas. After the Great Famine rural population fell drastically as people emigrated or moved to Dublin, Cork and Belfast, and it kept falling for over a century. The labourers' cottages scheme (1883-1936) helped only some areas. By the 1980s remote counties like Mayo, Donegal and Sligo still declined, while accessible towns like Maynooth grew by 16.6% (2011-2016). Today growth is mainly in the east and southeast. Young people leave because of a lack of jobs, poor transport and unreliable internet, leaving older communities; rural Ireland is about 35% of the population and greying faster than average. Schools, shops and post offices close. Project Ireland 2040, Our Rural Future and the RRDF aim to revive towns under 10,000 people.
